title: Michael Jones vs Lawrence Krauss: Christianity or Secular Ethics - What's Best for Society?
label: Christian social goods and secular inquiry
motion: Which is better for society: Christianity, understood as a Christian-value society with a largely Christian population, or secular ethics?
sourceNote: Assessment based exclusively on the complete locally cached YouTube caption transcript and timestamped events (transcript SHA-256 18fdc49b647b954f7db705fa22c8f8618eafa64e55767d8628f15d018383b562). Required below-high-confidence audio checks were completed before adjudication; representative quotations must be exact strings from quote-eligible locked source spans.
scoringNote: Scores are AI-generated estimates of argumentative performance under the locked adjudicated-consensus workflow. Repository code calculated every move, section, and overall result once, only after two isolated judgments, required audio review, and disputed-field adjudication closed.
summary: Christianity's institutional and moral arguments narrowly outperformed secular ethics, while secular challenges concerning heterogeneity, fallibilism, causation, and equal standing remained substantial.

pro.text: just because something happens in nature doesn't mean it's good
pro.context: Jones uses this descriptive-normative distinction to challenge attempts to derive moral value directly from animal behavior or biological facts.

con.text: there's a broad spectrum of Christians that believe in a lot of different things
con.context: Krauss questions whether heterogeneous Christian identities can support generalized correlations between Christianity and beneficial social outcomes.

pro.words: Christian missionary institutions and religious participation are associated with literacy, medical provision, charity, volunteering, democratic development, and other prosocial outcomes claimed to exceed secular alternatives.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The move directly addresses comparative social welfare through numerous concrete institutional and behavioral outcomes, giving the Christian route substantial breadth, empirical relevance, and recognizable public consequences. Principal limitation: It repeatedly merges missionary activity, religiosity, practiced Christianity, national Christianity, and secularization, while presenting summarized associations as comparatively decisive causal evidence without methodological qualification. Live burden: The argument still needs representative comparisons that separate selection effects, institutional inheritance, population heterogeneity, measurement choices, and specifically Christian mechanisms from generic participation or community integration. Locked score: The strong competent band reflects an important, evidence-oriented central contribution whose specificity and causal calibration remain materially weaker than its confident conclusion and extensive outcome inventory suggest.

con.words: Krauss disputes Christian social superiority by emphasizing missionary cultural damage, the scientific basis of useful medicine, contested studies, and the irrelevance of reproduction to cultural quality.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply directly contests central missionary and demographic inferences by separating scientific medicine from religious sponsorship, identifying possible cultural harms, and rejecting reproductive persistence as a quality metric. Principal limitation: It generalizes from alleged missionary damage and categorically assigns beneficial medicine to secular science without comparative documentation, while leaving the earlier authoritarianism evidence and several prosocial outcomes substantially unanswered. Live burden: The countercase must compare missions' benefits and harms, distinguish scientific method from institutional delivery, address the cited social research, and explain how secular arrangements reproduce equivalent charitable infrastructure. Locked score: The mixed band reflects meaningful contact with two important claims but also limited substantiation, incomplete responsiveness, categorical historical attribution, and insufficiently charitable treatment of potentially mixed missionary effects.

pro.words: A large research literature associates religiosity with better mental health and lower depression and suicide, which Jones presents as support for preferring Christian society over secularism.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Invoking a meta-analytic literature covering hundreds of studies supplies substantial evidential seriousness and connects the motion directly to depression, suicide, mental health, and population welfare. Principal limitation: The inference moves from religiosity to Christianity and from association to comparative causation, without effect sizes, methodological controls, denominational distinctions, confounding analysis, or acknowledged uncertainty. Live burden: The case must demonstrate that measured benefits are distinctively Christian, robust across populations, practically important, and not predominantly explained by social support, selection, reporting differences, or healthier participation. Locked score: The strong competent band recognizes a highly relevant empirical contribution while preserving substantial reservations about causal identification, category stability, comparative secular evidence, and the categorical confidence of the conclusion.

con.words: Broad religiosity and Christian labels cannot establish Christian social superiority when self-identified Christians represent sharply conflicting practices, moral commitments, and political positions.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply precisely diagnoses category heterogeneity and measurement specificity, showing why correlations involving religiosity or broad Christian labels cannot automatically support claims about a uniformly beneficial Christian society. Principal limitation: It demonstrates an important generalization problem but does not document the prevalence of conflicting subgroups, inspect the studies' coding, or determine whether narrower practiced-Christian measures actually retain the reported associations. Live burden: The challenge must connect its concrete internal counterexamples to the relevant datasets and establish how much the category defect changes each social, political, and mental-health inference. Locked score: The very strong band reflects explicit scope control, outstanding responsiveness, appropriate uncertainty, strong charity toward the narrower interpretation, and a diagnostically decisive objection whose empirical magnitude remains unresolved.

sections.title: Origins and Operation of Modern Institutions

pro.words: Medieval Christian legal traditions and Protestant missions are credited with important human-rights antecedents and substantial educational and health gains, challenging an exclusively secular account of modern progress.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The reply directly answers both historical attribution and missionary-benefit challenges with named scholarship, medieval legal antecedents, and institutional claims concerning education and health, producing unusually substantial responsive contact. Principal limitation: It sometimes moves from Christian contribution or chronological priority toward comparative predominance, without adequately distinguishing origin, later expansion, present justification, enforcement, secular operation, or interacting causes. Live burden: The case must show which modern rights and welfare institutions remain distinctively dependent on Christianity while incorporating secular reform, mixed missionary effects, joint development, and the possibility of independent contemporary justification. Locked score: The strong competent band reflects a well-supported, load-bearing full answer whose historical specificity and responsiveness are impressive, though its broader inference to Christian social superiority remains incomplete.

con.words: Krauss credits the liberal secular Enlightenment with modern knowledge and expanded moral concern after centuries of Christian dominance, including changed attitudes toward women, gay people, animals, and humanity.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The move supplies a clear secular historical narrative connecting Enlightenment inquiry, common ancestry, modern knowledge, and widened moral concern, directly advancing a central route for social progress. Principal limitation: It packages liberalism, secularism, science, and Enlightenment institutions together while attributing nearly all modern daily life to them through chronology rather than discriminating historical causation. Live burden: The account must separate independent secular innovation from development within inherited Christian institutions and evaluate reciprocal influence, legal antecedents, internal religious reform, and the later secular operation of shared institutions. Locked score: The mixed band recognizes breadth, relevance, and intelligible examples but reflects overstatement, limited historical demonstration, underdeveloped causal comparison, and insufficient engagement with the strongest Christian-antecedent explanation.

pro.words: Christian societies are credited with developing hospitals, orphanages, independent universities, church-state distinctions, and institutional conditions conducive to modern science, alongside continuing Christian healthcare provision.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The move supplies numerous recognizable institutional counterexamples to an exclusively secular progress narrative and combines historical development with the church's continuing worldwide healthcare provision. Principal limitation: Categorical claims that Christianity invented these institutions or enabled science overlook earlier precursors, internal diversity, historical continuity, joint development, and the distinction between institutional origins and modern operating methods. Live burden: The argument must establish comparative causal importance and present dependence, not merely Christian historical location, while addressing how secular governance, scientific standards, and pluralistic administration can sustain inherited institutions. Locked score: The strong competent band reflects direct, highly relevant full-answer responsiveness and substantial institutional evidence, tempered by overbroad authorship language, incomplete causal qualification, and limited engagement with reciprocal reform.

con.words: Natural science's insistence that physical effects have physical causes is credited with displacing supernatural accusations such as witchcraft and demonstrating secular inquiry's socially corrective power.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The move provides a vivid mechanism through which natural explanation can displace supernatural blame, connecting scientific intelligibility to reduced persecution and concrete social correction. Principal limitation: The asserted timing between Newtonian science and declining witch burning does not establish causation, distinctively secular agency, magnitude, or exclusion of theological, legal, political, and economic alternatives. Live burden: The reply must substantiate the historical sequence and mechanism while answering the targeted claims that Christian doctrines and institutions contributed to experimentation, scientific method, and the conditions permitting natural philosophy. Locked score: The mixed band recognizes a relevant and intelligible secular benefit but reflects its classification as a relevant nonanswer, underdeveloped causal history, incomplete target contact, and only partial accommodation of plausible co-causes.

sections.title: Foundations of Morality, Dignity, and Cooperation

pro.words: Facts about animal behavior or biological nature cannot alone determine moral value, and claims that conduct is natural must distinguish biological description from natural-law theory.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The response precisely identifies the descriptive-normative gap, explains why observed animal behavior cannot alone establish goodness, and carefully distinguishes biological nature from natural-law terminology. Principal limitation: Its diagnostic success defeats only a bare inference from natural occurrence to moral value, not empirically informed secular ethics that separately adopts normative commitments concerning suffering, reciprocity, autonomy, or equal regard. Live burden: The Christian case must supply its own positive bridge to moral obligation while showing that the opposing account actually depends decisively on biological description rather than using common humanity as supporting evidence. Locked score: The very strong band reflects exceptional logical precision, explicit qualification, direct responsiveness, and fair acknowledgment of boundaries, with only the limited scope of the diagnostic conclusion remaining.

con.words: Secular ethics can ground moral life through equal regard, rational inquiry, sympathy, conscientious perspective-taking, and empathy for everyone affected by one's choices without requiring belief in God.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The move directly supplies a secular ethical foundation through sympathy, perspective-taking, equal regard, rational reflection, and conscientious attention to affected people, rather than merely criticizing religious morality. Principal limitation: Its philosophical examples establish the availability and coherence of secular ethics more clearly than their motivational reliability, institutional durability, or resolution of conflicts among welfare, rights, and competing interests. Live burden: The framework must explain how equal consideration adjudicates hard tradeoffs, why agents remain obligated when sympathy weakens, and how public institutions translate empathy into stable, revisable, generally applicable norms. Locked score: The strong competent band reflects exceptionally direct burden fulfillment, stable terminology, appropriate calibration, and charitable acknowledgment of overlap with Jesus, while leaving practical and metaethical questions legitimately open.

pro.words: Christian abolitionist teaching about common Adamic ancestry and one human family is presented as an important influence on Darwin's conception of human unity and equality.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The reply names historians, texts, a transmission route, and a bounded intellectual influence, directly challenging the claim that Darwinian human unity arose independently from Christian abolitionist thought. Principal limitation: Historical influence on Darwin does not establish that Christianity uniquely grounds equality, that current secular justification depends on that ancestry, or that broad credit follows from one documented pathway. Live burden: The argument must distinguish intellectual genealogy from normative validity and show how Adamic unity contributed comparatively across institutions, populations, and reform movements while confronting Christian traditions that resisted equal treatment. Locked score: The strong competent band reflects specific evidence, strong target contact, stable scope, and effective historical rebuttal, tempered by somewhat expanded causal credit and incomplete engagement with present secular adequacy.

con.words: Secular ethics affirms equal standing and social claims through common humanity and demonstrated biological kinship, without treating scriptural authority as necessary for human worth.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The move clearly affirms equal standing, happiness, survival, and social care, supplying a positive secular moral commitment instead of relying exclusively on criticism of Christian foundations. Principal limitation: Scientific evidence of shared humanity and DNA establishes factual kinship but cannot independently entail equal rights, obligations, or social provision without an additional normative premise that remains mostly implicit. Live burden: The account must articulate that normative bridge, explain its authority and application, and show how common humanity supports equal treatment amid conflicting interests, scarce resources, partiality, and disagreement. Locked score: The strong competent band reflects direct central relevance, stable concepts, substantial coherence, and charitable preservation of the qualification, while recognizing incomplete responsiveness to the fact-to-value objection.

pro.words: Original sin is reframed as teaching human fallibility, which reportedly encouraged early scientists to repeat experiments and verify results during the development of scientific method.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The reply offers a concrete and historically intelligible mechanism linking original sin to epistemic fallibility, repeated experimentation, verification, and the development of scientific practice. Principal limitation: Although relevant to Christianity's intellectual effects, it does not answer the targeted objections about inherited guilt, eternal punishment, coercive condemnation, or the alleged impossibility of moral self-correction. Live burden: The response must preserve its historical contribution claim while separately confronting punitive doctrine, determining the breadth of the influence among scientists, and distinguishing contribution from necessity or predominant causal credit. Locked score: The mixed band reflects coherent reasoning, named historical support, and useful doctrinal reinterpretation, but also partial responsiveness, somewhat overstated historical importance, and failure to contact the criticism's decisive punishment component.

con.words: A secular ethos of accepting error, human responsibility, naturalized choice, and cosmic humility is offered as support for an open and humane society without supernatural supervision.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The move presents responsibility, error admission, openness, and cosmic humility as a coherent secular disposition, offering an intelligible safeguard against certainty and uncorrectable authority. Principal limitation: It moves from a personal naturalistic outlook to reliable institutional humaneness without demonstrating the mechanism, while describing religion through cosmic dictatorship and solipsism rather than its strongest accountability interpretation. Live burden: The argument must show how secular fallibilism becomes durable practice, constrains dogmatic political movements, and performs comparatively better than religious traditions that also teach humility, responsibility, and human limitation. Locked score: The mixed band reflects conceptual coherence and plausible normative value but also subsidiary burden contact, modest empirical warrant, broad social extrapolation, and a materially incomplete representation of religious alternatives.

pro.words: Christian beliefs concerning fallible humanity, lawful creation, and an intelligible natural order are presented as mechanisms that materially encouraged experimentation, verification, and scientific method.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The move specifies several plausible intellectual mechanisms connecting Christian doctrine to science, including human fallibility, repeated verification, lawful creation, and confidence that nature is intelligible. Principal limitation: It does not establish the magnitude, representativeness, independence, or necessity of these influences, and broad references to Christianity and scientific method conceal considerable historical diversity and multiple intellectual traditions. Live burden: The argument must demonstrate transmission into scientific practice, compare rival causal sources, identify affected communities and periods, and distinguish meaningful contribution from indispensable foundation or continuing religious dependence. Locked score: The strong competent band reflects coherent mechanism, stable central terminology, relevant historical support, and appropriate contribution-level force, while retaining reservations about causal scale, comparative evidence, and unacknowledged alternative pathways.

con.words: Christian teachings about inherited sin and eternal punishment are criticized as imposing impossible guilt and coercively condemning nonbelief or the exercise of individual choice.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The move identifies a specific doctrinal pathway from inherited sin and eternal punishment to guilt, coercion, and psychological harm, making Christianity's possible social costs concrete and morally important. Principal limitation: It treats a particularly punitive interpretation as representative Christianity and amplifies it through extreme language without distinguishing denominational teachings, grace-centered accounts, metaphorical readings, or actual social prevalence. Live burden: The criticism must compare interpretations and practices, establish how frequently the alleged mechanism operates, and separate the concerns about inherited guilt, impossible self-cure, childhood instruction, nonbelief, and eternal punishment. Locked score: The mixed band reflects substantial relevance and a recognizable coercion objection but also weak representational charity, broad doctrinal generalization, limited social evidence, and force exceeding the supplied warrant.

pro.words: Practiced Christianity is presented as restraining Christian nationalism and rival political religions while supporting citizen empowerment, accountability, democratic values, human rights, and resistance to corruption.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The move connects Christian practice to accountability, democratic values, human rights, citizen empowerment, and reduced corruption, thereby engaging political liberty through concrete and socially consequential criteria. Principal limitation: Its categories remain unstable, and the prediction that secularization generates Christian nationalism, wokeism, or comparable political religions receives neither representative evidence nor adequate causal explanation. Live burden: The argument must distinguish practiced Christianity from Christian identity, address ordinary democratic secularism, and show across relevant populations that religious practice restrains rather than sometimes accompanies authoritarian mobilization. Locked score: The mixed band reflects strong relevance and identifiable empirical direction but also materially overstated causation, incomplete operational definitions, selective alternatives, and insufficient comparative support for the political forecast.

con.words: Krauss challenges Christian credit for women's rights through Christianity's historical restrictions on women and rejects demographic pessimism by citing rapid world population growth.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply contacts both selected demands by highlighting Christianity's historically mixed treatment of women and disputing the proposition that demographic persistence establishes social superiority. Principal limitation: Aggregate world population growth does not answer replacement fertility among secular subpopulations, while dismissing Christian contributions to women's rights categorically fails to assess contradictory institutions, actors, periods, and causal pathways. Live burden: The response needs subgroup demographic evidence, a defensible account of cultural continuity, and a comparative history that weighs Christian restrictions against Christian reformers, secular movements, legal change, and institutional interaction. Locked score: The mixed band reflects high relevance and direct engagement but also weak demographic warrant, overconfident historical dismissal, incomplete category matching, and limited charity toward a genuinely mixed causal record.

pro.words: Jones argues that beneficial cultures require intergenerational demographic continuity and that historically higher Christian fertility better preserves Christian institutions than below-replacement secular populations can.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The argument identifies intergenerational continuity as a distinct social requirement and candidly concedes that secular culture may presently deliver well-being, thereby focusing attention on long-term institutional preservation. Principal limitation: It treats adherent replacement fertility as necessary for cultural survival without establishing comparative rates, relevant time horizons, or why migration, conversion, transmission, and institutional adaptation are inadequate. Live burden: The case must connect demographic persistence to preservation of the specified benefits while distinguishing current adherents, descendants, cultural influence, institutional continuity, and the quality of whatever culture eventually replaces them. Locked score: The mixed band records genuine motion relevance and a coherent continuity concern but also sparse evidence, an overextended necessity claim, and incomplete engagement with major nonbiological mechanisms.

con.words: Christianity is said to have become gentler because liberal scientific Enlightenment institutions protected disagreement and constrained inherited religion, reversing claims that Christianity principally created modern freedom.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply offers a clear causal reversal, arguing that liberal scientific institutions moderated Christianity and secured freedom, while directly contacting Christian claims about institutions, authoritarian restraint, and rights. Principal limitation: Its near-exclusive reform story relies heavily on historical sequence and broad categories, underweighting reciprocal influence, internal Christian reform, religiously motivated liberalization, and institutional development spanning both traditions. Live burden: The secular account must identify mechanisms, comparative cases, and temporal evidence showing that liberal constraints produced the relevant changes independently enough to support priority rather than merely interaction or mutual adaptation. Locked score: The strong competent band reflects excellent responsiveness, coherent explanatory competition, and central relevance, tempered by limited evidential warrant, categorical causal language, and insufficiently plural historical attribution.

strengths: The institutional-history case landed through named scholarship, concrete medieval rights antecedents, missionary education and health claims, and continuing Christian healthcare provision.
The naturalistic-fallacy reply precisely separated biological description from moral evaluation and directly exposed an unresolved normative bridge in the secular equality argument.

The Christian case offered identifiable doctrinal mechanisms for science, connecting fallibility, verification, lawful creation, and natural intelligibility rather than relying only on historical coincidence.
The Adamic-unity reply supplied a specific intellectual pathway from Christian abolitionism to Darwin's conception of a single human family.

blunders.text: The social-outcomes case repeatedly treated religiosity, practiced Christianity, missionary activity, and Christian society as interchangeable categories despite their substantial empirical heterogeneity.

The fertility argument presented biological replacement as necessary for cultural continuity without addressing migration, conversion, transmission, institutional adaptation, or changing secular fertility patterns.

strengths: The secular ethical basis landed as a positive account grounded in sympathy, conscientious perspective-taking, equal regard, and concern for people affected by choices.
The heterogeneity challenge sharply exposed why generic religiosity findings and broad Christian labels cannot automatically establish Christian society's comparative superiority.

The secular-reform reply offered a coherent rival causal direction in which liberal institutions constrained religion and protected disagreement, directly engaging several Christian historical claims.
The equal-standing argument clearly denied that scriptural authority is necessary for affirming universal moral status and social concern.

blunders.text: The Enlightenment narrative attributed nearly all modern progress to an insufficiently differentiated package of secularism, liberalism, science, and historical chronology.
The demographic reply used total world population growth to answer the narrower issue of replacement fertility and cultural persistence among secular populations.
The sin-and-punishment criticism generalized a particularly punitive Christian interpretation while neglecting grace-centered, denominational, and nonliteral alternatives.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that a broadly Christian society can be socially advantageous when its doctrines sustain an institutional ecology of equal dignity, fallibility, service, voluntary association, and intergenerational responsibility while remaining open to empirical correction.
premises: Christian participation should be defended through carefully matched evidence about practiced communities, institutional participation, and specified outcomes, without equating every religious measure or self-identified Christian population.

Hospitals, universities, charities, missions, and rights traditions can matter as accumulated institutional capital even when their contemporary methods are scientific and their governance is religiously pluralistic.

Christian anthropology can support public correction when human fallibility applies equally to clergy, rulers, scientists, and believers, making criticism and institutional checks religious responsibilities rather than threats.

Equal human worth can be grounded in a theological commitment to one human family, while empirical knowledge informs consequences and application without being asked to generate moral obligation by itself.
Cultural continuity is best pursued through education, persuasion, family support, service, and institutional excellence rather than treating adherent fertility alone as necessary or sufficient.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, society has a qualified reason to preserve and encourage Christian institutions where they demonstrably cultivate service, dignity, fallibility, freedom, and durable voluntary communities, while continuously testing those effects and correcting coercive or exclusionary practices.

newArguments.title: Covenantal accountability as distributed governance
newArguments.text: A Christian society could argue that covenantal responsibility creates accountability at several levels simultaneously: persons answer for conduct, congregations discipline leaders, voluntary associations serve local needs, and public institutions remain subject to moral criticism. This distributed structure can reduce dependence on a single central authority and preserve social trust when government capacity is limited. The claim is conditional, because churches can themselves become coercive; its force therefore depends on transparent governance, pluralism, independent law, and measurable service beyond insiders.

newArguments.title: Costly service as institutional credibility
newArguments.text: Christian practices of regular giving, volunteering, caregiving, and long-term membership may provide a costly signal of commitment that helps charitable institutions recruit dependable participants. The relevant comparison is not belief versus unbelief in the abstract, but whether communities create repeatable norms that lower coordination costs and sustain service through crises. This argument can be tested without assuming supernatural truth: researchers could compare retention, beneficiary reach, outsider service, governance quality, and durability across matched religious and secular organizations.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that secular ethics offers the better public framework when equal standing, empathy, open criticism, and evidence-sensitive institutions provide revisable common rules without making citizenship depend on contested theology.
premises: Equal moral standing should be stated as an independent public commitment: shared biology identifies who belongs to humanity, but the principle of equal consideration supplies the normative obligation.

Empathy becomes a durable ethic when institutions translate perspective-taking into general rights, transparent procedures, welfare protections, and reasons that can be challenged by everyone affected.

Secular fallibilism is institutionally valuable when claims remain answerable to public evidence, peaceful dissent, independent inquiry, and procedures that permit correction without requiring theological agreement.

A secular society can acknowledge Christian contributions to hospitals, universities, rights, and reform while maintaining that inherited institutions now receive justification from accessible public purposes and empirical performance.

Religious and secular organizations should be judged by comparable evidence concerning inclusion, coercion, service, welfare, freedom, and correction rather than by labels, ancestry, or aggregate demographic persistence.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, secular ethics provides a proportionate basis for public institutions when it explicitly affirms equal consideration, converts empathy into rights and procedures, protects open correction, and evaluates religious and nonreligious organizations by the same evidence-sensitive standards.

newArguments.title: Public reason under persistent disagreement
newArguments.text: A plural society needs decisions that remain explainable to citizens who reasonably disagree about revelation, salvation, and metaphysics. Secular ethics can serve as a common public language by asking officials to justify coercive rules through shared interests, evidence, rights, and reciprocally applicable reasons. Religious citizens retain full freedom to contribute their convictions, but public authority must translate proposals into terms open to challenge by everyone. This arrangement reduces domination without declaring theology false and makes peaceful revision possible after evidence or social understanding changes.

newArguments.title: Competing institutions for error correction
newArguments.text: Secular society can strengthen fallibilism by maintaining several independent correction systems: free journalism, adversarial courts, open science, democratic opposition, professional review, and protected civil society. Their disagreement is productive because no institution controls every channel through which errors become visible. Religious organizations can participate and flourish within this structure, but none receives exemption from public evidence or general law. The comparative advantage lies in institutional redundancy, not an assumption that secular individuals are personally humbler or morally superior.
